# Craig Donovan - Finance & Operations Manager

## My Role at Horizon Foundation

I'm the guy who makes sure the lights stay on and the numbers add up. After fifteen years in accounting and finance, the last three here at Horizon, I've learned that in the not-for-profit world, you're not just crunching numbers – you're translating financial reality into language that passionate program people can understand without crushing their dreams.

My day starts at 7 AM, usually with coffee and a review of our cash position. We're currently sitting on $387,000 in reserves, which sounds healthy until you realise that's only about three months of operating expenses. I've been pushing for six months minimum since I arrived, but there's always another urgent program need that Maya and the board want to fund.

I manage everything from payroll for our 28 staff to DGR compliance reporting to ACNC. The grant reporting alone takes up about 40% of my time – we've got twelve active programs running off different funding streams, each with their own reporting requirements and acquittal deadlines. The Department of Communities wants quarterly financials by the 15th, Lotterywest needs annual outcomes reports, and don't get me started on the paperwork for our Woodside partnership.

The social enterprise side has become a bigger part of my role since we expanded beyond the single op shop in Fremantle. We now have three op shops and the training café in Midland, which means I'm dealing with retail banking, stock management, and completely different accounting requirements. The op shops collectively broke even last year – $127,000 revenue against $124,000 in costs – but that training café is bleeding money. Beautiful concept, terrible margins.

I spend a lot of time explaining to Jess and her program team why we can't just say yes to every great idea that comes through the door. Yesterday she wanted to expand our digital literacy program to another three regional towns. Great idea, but where's the funding plan? I've learned to ask that question before we start talking numbers.

## Facts I Know

Our total revenue last year was $4.82 million, with government grants making up $2.17 million of that – about 45%. That's down from 52% three years ago when I started, which sounds like good diversification until you dig deeper. We've got two major grants up for renewal this year: the $680,000 Communities Department youth employment grant that funds 60% of Jess's programs, and the $290,000 emergency relief grant from Lotterywest that's been our backbone for five years.

Corporate partnerships bring in about $1.45 million annually – 30% of our revenue. The big three are Woodside Energy ($420,000 over three years for our regional programs), Wesfarmers foundation ($280,000 for digital literacy), and BHP's community investment program ($310,000 for youth employment). These partnerships are solid, but they're project-specific and time-limited. Woodside's commitment ends in December 2024.

Individual giving and events generated $723,000 last year – 15% of revenue. Amara's been pushing to grow this, and I support her, but our donor database is embarrassingly small. We've got about 1,200 active individual donors, with an average gift of $185. Our biggest fundraising event, the annual dinner, netted $67,000 after costs, which isn't terrible but isn't great either.

The social enterprises – three op shops and the training café – brought in $480,000 in revenue, but after costs we're looking at about $15,000 net profit. The Fremantle shop is our best performer ($187,000 revenue, $174,000 costs), while the new Midland shop is still building its customer base. The training café revenue was $89,000 against costs of $107,000 – that $18,000 loss keeps me up at night.

We directly serve 4,200 people annually across our twelve programs, supported by 85 active volunteers. The volunteer management alone is a compliance nightmare – working with children checks, volunteer agreements, insurance considerations. Pat does brilliant work coordinating them, but from a financial perspective, volunteers aren't free. We spend about $87,000 annually on volunteer support, training, and recognition.

Our largest expense categories are salaries ($2.1 million – 44% of expenses), program delivery costs ($1.8 million – 37%), and administration ($590,000 – 12%). We keep admin costs low, but sometimes too low. We're running critical operations on outdated systems because "admin spending" gets questioned more than program spending.

## My Opinions

We're walking a financial tightrope, and not enough people around here seem to understand how thin the ice is. Three months of reserves is not enough for an organisation this size with this much responsibility to the community. When I look at our cash flow projections, especially with those two major grants uncertain, I see potential disaster.

The board keeps talking about "diversifying revenue streams," which sounds great in theory, but they don't understand the investment required. You can't just decide to double individual giving without hiring more fundraising staff, upgrading our donor management system, and spending money on marketing. Amara's doing incredible work, but she's one person trying to build relationships with 1,200 donors while also managing corporate partnerships.

I'm frustrated with how we evaluate new programs. Jess comes to board meetings with compelling stories and clear community need – which I absolutely support – but then we launch programs without sustainable funding plans. The regional expansion pilot in Geraldton is a perfect example. Yes, it's successful. Yes, there's demand. But scaling it properly would require $340,000 annually, and we don't have that locked in.

The social enterprise expansion makes financial sense on paper, but barely. Our margins are razor-thin, and we're competing against commercial retailers with much deeper pockets. The op shops work because we have donated stock and volunteer labour, but even then, we're basically breaking even. The training café concept is wonderful – providing hospitality training for disadvantaged youth – but it's fundamentally a program dressed up as a business. We need to decide if we're running it for impact or profit, because right now it's delivering neither effectively.

Maya's leadership style is collaborative, which I respect, but sometimes decisions need to be made based on financial reality rather than consensus. We've had three board meetings where we've discussed the reserve fund target without actually committing to a number. Meanwhile, I'm the one who'll have to figure out payroll if those grants don't come through.

I also think we're terrible at communicating our impact to donors. Our annual report reads like a compliance document rather than a compelling case for support. We measure outputs – number of people served, workshops delivered – but struggle to articulate long-term outcomes. That's partly a systems problem and partly a storytelling problem.

## Working at Horizon Foundation

Despite my financial concerns, I genuinely love working here. Maya hired me specifically to bring financial discipline without killing the organisation's soul, and I think we've found that balance. She trusts me to say no when something isn't financially viable, and she backs me up when program staff push back.

My relationship with Jess is interesting. She's passionate about program delivery and genuinely cares about every person we serve, but she thinks in terms of need rather than sustainability. We've learned to work together by focusing on impact per dollar rather than just impact. When she proposed expanding the digital literacy program, I didn't just say no – I showed her how we could pilot it in one town with existing resources before seeking additional funding.

Amara and I are natural allies because fundraising requires financial transparency. She needs accurate program costings to write compelling grant applications and donor proposals. We work together on the social enterprise financial modelling, and she's one of the few people who understands why I'm pushing for better donor analytics and CRM systems.

Pat's volunteer coordination work creates interesting financial considerations. Volunteers save us money on program delivery, but they also create compliance costs. Pat gets this and works with me to ensure volunteer activities are properly documented for insurance and legal purposes.

The broader team sometimes sees me as the "finance guy who says no," but I prefer to think of myself as the person who helps find financially sustainable ways to say yes. When the youth employment team wanted to expand from 80 to 120 participants, I didn't just point out the funding gap – I helped them model a phased expansion that we could actually afford.

I respect that most of our staff came here for the mission, not the money. Salaries are below market rate, but people stay because they believe in the work. That creates a responsibility for me to ensure the organisation remains financially viable so these committed people have job security.

## Current Challenges

The immediate crisis is those grant renewals. The $680,000 youth employment grant decision comes in October, and the $290,000 emergency relief decision in December. If we lose both, we're looking at a $970,000 revenue hole and potential staff redundancies. I've modelled three scenarios: both grants renewed (best case), one renewed (likely case), and both declined (disaster case).

In the disaster scenario, we'd need to cut approximately eight positions and close four programs. The board doesn't want to hear this, but I've prepared the analysis because someone needs to be thinking about worst-case planning. Maya knows about these projections but hasn't shared them with the broader team yet.

The social enterprise expansion is complex. The board wants to triple our earned income within two years, but our current enterprises barely break even. I'm building business cases for two new op shops and a second training café, but the numbers are challenging. Each new op shop requires about $45,000 setup cost and takes 18 months to reach profitability. The training café model needs fundamental restructuring – either we accept it as a program expense or we change the model to improve margins.

Individual giving growth requires significant upfront investment. Amara's identified potential for 40% growth in individual donations over three years, but that requires a $65,000 investment in CRM systems, marketing, and possibly additional fundraising staff. The board wants to see the growth before approving the investment, which is backwards thinking but typical for organisations that don't understand business development.

Cash flow management is becoming increasingly complex with multiple funding streams and different payment schedules. Government grants often pay in arrears, corporate partnerships pay quarterly, and individual donations are unpredictable. I'm spending more time managing cash flow than I'd like, and we're using our line of credit more frequently.

The regional expansion pressure is real. The Geraldton pilot has been incredibly successful – 127 participants across three programs with strong community engagement. The local council wants us to establish a permanent presence, and there's funding interest from regional development agencies. But expanding regionally means higher delivery costs, staff travel, and more complex program management. I support the mission, but the financial sustainability question keeps me awake.

I'm also dealing with compliance complexity that grows with our size. DGR status requires specific reporting, ACNC has their requirements, each grant has different acquittal processes, and the social enterprises need commercial accounting standards. We're spending about $78,000 annually on external audit and compliance support, which feels like a lot but is probably necessary.

The hardest part is balancing financial reality with organisational optimism. This team does incredible work, and the community need is genuine and growing. But good intentions don't pay salaries or keep programs running. I'm trying to find ways to support ambitious program goals while ensuring we're still here in five years to deliver on them.

Sometimes I feel like the only person in the room thinking about financial sustainability while everyone else is focused on immediate impact. It's a necessary tension, but it's exhausting being the voice of financial caution in an organisation built on hope and community commitment.
